en: Majjhima Nikāya 53,
Sekhasutta.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Now at that time a new assembly hall had recently been built for the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, which had not yet been occupied by any ascetic, brahmin, or human being whatsoever.
Then the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu approached the Blessed One; having approached, they [paid homage to] the Blessed One...
Having paid homage, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, here is a new assembly hall belonging to the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, recently built and not yet inhabited by any ascetic, brahmin, or human being.
May the Blessed One be the first to use it; when the Blessed One has used it first, afterwards the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu will use it.”
"That will be for the long-term welfare and happiness of the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from their seats and [approached] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage and circumambulated him, they approached the new assembly hall.
Having arrived, they spread a complete carpet over the assembly hall, prepared seats, set out water jars, and lit oil lamps.
Then they approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, the assembly hall has been spread with a complete carpet; seats have been prepared; a water-jar has been set out; and an oil lamp has been raised."
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One do as he deems timely.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, approached the assembly hall together with the community of monks.
Having arrived, he washed his feet, entered the assembly hall, and [stood] by the central pillar.
He sat down leaning against the eastern wall, facing eastward.
The community of monks also washed their feet, entered the assembly hall, and sat down leaning against the western wall, facing eastward, with the Blessed One before them.
The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu also washed their feet, entered the assembly hall, and sat down leaning against the eastern wall, facing westward, with the Blessed One before them.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu for much of the night with a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, let a discourse on the practice of the learner occur to you regarding the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu.
My back is aching.”
“I shall attend upon him.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe folded fourfold, lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, with his mind fixed on the thought of rising.
Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed Mahānāma the Sakyan:
“In this case, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is accomplished in virtue, guards the doors of his sense faculties,
is moderate in eating, is devoted to wakefulness, possesses the seven good qualities, and [is endowed with] the four...”
He is one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
And how, Mahānāma, is a noble disciple accomplished in virtue?

Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
In this way, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is accomplished in virtue.
And how, Mahānāma, is a noble disciple guarded in the doors of the sense faculties?
Here, Mahānāma, having seen a form with the eye, a noble disciple does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the eye, he achieves restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe… having touched a tangible object with the body …pe…
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of mind unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of mind and achieves restraint over the faculty of mind.
In this way, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is one whose sense doors are guarded.
And how, Mahānāma, is a noble disciple moderate in eating?
Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple reflects wisely before partaking of food:
‘Neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for adornment, nor for beautification, but only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body,
for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life (brahmacariya).
Thus I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.’
In this way, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is moderate in eating.
And how, Mahānāma, is a noble disciple devoted to wakefulness?
Here, Mahānāma, during the day, while walking back and forth and sitting, a noble disciple purifies his mind of obstructive states.
During the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking meditation and sitting.

During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his attention on the perception of rising.
During the last watch of the night, having risen, he purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking meditation and sitting.
In this way, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is devoted to wakefulness.
And how, Mahānāma, is a noble disciple endowed with the seven true qualities?
Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is possessed of faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

He is possessed of a sense of shame; he feels shame at bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he feels shame at the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states. He is possessed of moral dread;
he dreads bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he dreads the undertaking of evil, unwholesome states.
He is learned, one who has retained what he has heard, and one who has accumulated what he has heard. Those teachings which are good in the beginning,
good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the holy life that is entirely perfect and pure—
such teachings as these are well-learned by him, mastered verbally, thoroughly investigated by the mind, and well-penetrated through vision.

He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish his burden regarding wholesome states.
He is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection, one who remembers and recalls what was done long ago and spoken long ago.
He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
"In this way, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is possessed of the seven true qualities.
And how, Mahānāma, does a noble disciple obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the four jhānas that are higher mental states, providing a dwelling in happiness in this very life?
Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...enters and dwells in the first jhāna."
With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind...
with the fading away of rapture... he enters and dwells in the third jhāna...
with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

In this way, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without toil, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
When, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is thus perfected in virtue, thus has his sense faculties guarded,
thus knows moderation in eating, thus is devoted to wakefulness, and thus possesses the seven true qualities—

When he is thus possessed [of these qualities], he becomes one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
Mahānāma, such a noble disciple is called a trainee (sekha) practicing the path, who has attained freedom from impetuosity;
he is capable of breaking out, capable of full enlightenment, and capable of [liberation].
for the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Just as, Mahānāma, if there were eight, ten, or twelve eggs of a hen, and they were properly sat upon by the hen,
properly incubated, and properly brooded— then even though for that hen...
Even if the wish were not to arise:
"Oh, may these chicks break out of their shells with the tips of their claws or the points of their beaks and emerge safely," nevertheless,
those chicks are indeed capable of breaking out of their shells with the tips of their claws or the points of their beaks and emerging safely.
In the same way, Mahānāma, when a noble disciple is thus perfected in virtue, thus guards the doors of the sense faculties,
thus is moderate in eating, thus is devoted to wakefulness, thus is endowed with the seven true qualities,
and thus possesses the four jhānas— states of higher mind that provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life—
He obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble; this, Mahānāma, is called a noble disciple who is a trainee (sekha) practicing the path,
who has attained freedom from cruelty, who is capable of breaking out, capable of enlightenment,
and capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.
"Mahānāma, it is by relying on this very supreme purity of mindfulness through equanimity that a noble disciple recollects his manifold past abodes, such as one birth, two births...
[as before] ...thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
This is his first breakthrough, like that of a chick from its eggshell."
In this very way, Mahānāma, that noble disciple, by relying on this unsurpassed purity of mindfulness through equanimity,
with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, sees beings passing away and being reborn—
low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
This is his second breakthrough, like that of a chick from its eggshell. Now, Mahānāma,
by relying on this very supreme purity of mindfulness through equanimity, that noble disciple,
through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
Having realized it and attained it, he dwells therein;
this is his third breakthrough, like that of a chick from its eggshell.
Furthermore, Mahānāma, when a noble disciple is accomplished in virtue, this too constitutes his conduct.
Furthermore, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple guards the doors of the sense faculties—this too is part of his conduct;
furthermore, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple is moderate in eating—this too is part of his conduct;
furthermore, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple is devoted to wakefulness—this too is part of his conduct.
Furthermore, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple is endowed with seven true qualities—this too is part of his conduct.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple is one who gains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life—this too is part of his conduct.
And furthermore, Mahānāma, that a noble disciple recollects his manifold past abodes, such as: even one [life]...
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... [as above] ...thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives;
this too, Mahānāma, is his true knowledge.
Furthermore, Mahānāma, a noble disciple, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, beholds beings...
He sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
This, too, is his true knowledge (*vijjā*).

Furthermore, Mahānāma, when a noble disciple, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself through direct higher knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwells therein—this, too, is his true knowledge.

“Mahānāma, this noble disciple is called one who is accomplished in true knowledge (*vijjā*), one who is accomplished in conduct (*caraṇa*), and one who is accomplished in both true knowledge and conduct.
Mahānāma, even this verse was spoken by the Brahmā Sanankumāra:
‘The kṣatriya is the best among people…’”
Those who rely on their clan;
but one perfected in true knowledge and conduct is the best among gods and humans.”
“Moreover, Mahānāma, this verse was well-sung, not ill-sung, well-spoken, not ill-spoken, endowed with meaning, not devoid of meaning, by Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra; it has been approved by the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having risen, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!”
"It is well indeed, Ānanda, that you have spoken to the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu about the path of training.
This is what the Venerable Ānanda said.
The Teacher approved.
The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu were delighted and rejoiced in the Venerable Ānanda’s words.
The third sutta, the Sekhasutta, is concluded.
